a: Baruch wrote in Babylon
p: Baruch is Jeremiah's scribe. Jeremiah's own book puts him in Egypt after 586 BC, not in Babylon.
b: The family line matches Jeremiah: "Baruch son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah" (Jeremiah 32:12). There Baruch writes down Jeremiah's words and reads the scroll aloud in the temple (Jeremiah 36:4, 10), as here he reads a book aloud to the exiles. But when Jerusalem fell, Jeremiah's book says the survivors "also took Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah" to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:6). Nothing in the 66 books puts him in Babylon. Francis Gigot, writing for the Catholic Encyclopedia, noted that a Jewish tradition kept by Jerome has Baruch die in Egypt, which "conflicts with" this chapter. Crawford Toy, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, saw no reason to think Baruch was ever in Babylon. Those who hold the book as Scripture answer that Baruch could have gone east later, and that the frame should be read for what it teaches. The book's opening pages weigh the authorship views.
r: Jeremiah 32:12; Jeremiah 36:4; Jeremiah 36:10; Jeremiah 43:6; Jeremiah 45:1; Jeremiah 51:59

a: the fifth year, the seventh day of the month
p: The Greek names a year and a day but no month, and does not say from what the year is counted.
b: The Greek reads "in the fifth year, on the seventh of the month". The month is missing, and so is the starting point of the count. The fall of Jerusalem gives one possible key: the city was burned "on the seventh day of the fifth month" (2 Kings 25:8), so the writer may be marking the anniversary of the burning, in the fifth year after it. Another way to count is Ezekiel's, who dates his visions by "the exile of King Jehoiachin" (Ezekiel 1:2), the king who hears this book in 1:3. Toy called the date obscure and thought the second way more likely. Either way the frame sets the book in the years after 586 BC, among exiles who remembered the burning.

a: Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah
p: Jeconiah is King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC and kept there for 37 years.
b: Jeconiah (Greek Iechonias) is another form of the name Jehoiachin; Jeremiah's book uses both (Jeremiah 24:1; Jeremiah 52:31). He surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar after three months as king and was taken to Babylon with his household and the leading men (2 Kings 24:12–15). He was still in Babylon when Evil-merodach released him from prison in the thirty-seventh year of his exile (2 Kings 25:27). So the frame has the right king in the right city. It makes the exiled king the first hearer of a confession of the nation's sins, and so the whole people, from the king to the least, take part in it (1:4).

a: by the river Sud
p: No other text names a river Sud. One suggestion is that it is a miscopied Kebar, Ezekiel's canal.
b: Babylonia was crossed by the Euphrates and by many canals, and exiles lived along them: Ezekiel was "among the exiles by the Kebar canal" (Ezekiel 1:1), and a psalm remembers weeping "beside the rivers of Babylon" (Psalm 137:1). A river Sud is not known from any other source. The Latin has Sodi. Toy called it "enigmatical" and suggested that it may be a miswriting of Kebar. This cannot be checked, and the Plain keeps the name the Greek gives.

a: They wept and fasted
p: The exiles mourn as Judeans did for Jerusalem: with weeping, fasting and prayer.
b: After 586 BC Judeans kept fasts for the city's fall; Zechariah's hearers had "fasted and mourned in the fifth month and the seventh" for seventy years (Zechariah 7:5), and the fifth-month fast remembers the burning of the temple (2 Kings 25:8). Baruch's frame shows the same response far from the land: the exiles weep, fast and pray, then send gifts and a written confession home. The scene gives later readers a pattern for a community that has lost its temple: grief turned into prayer and into practical help for Jerusalem.

a: the priest Joakim son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum
p: The priestly lists name no Joakim son of Hilkiah. The Greek name is the same as King Jehoiakim's.
b: The Greek Iōakeim is the same name the book gives King Jehoiakim in 1:3; the Plain writes "Joakim" for the priest so the reader can tell them apart. Shallum and Hilkiah are known high priests: "Shallum fathered Hilkiah, and Hilkiah fathered Azariah", and the line runs on to Seraiah and Jehozadak (1 Chronicles 6:13–14). Seraiah, "the head priest", was taken by the Babylonians in 586 BC (Jeremiah 52:24), and Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chronicles 6:15). No Joakim appears in the list. The Greek calls him only "the priest" here, so readers who take the frame as history can read him as a leading priest left in Judah, not the high priest. Readers who see the frame as later fiction note that the high priest of Judith is also called Joakim.

a: That was when Baruch took
p: The Greek says only "when he took". The Plain names Baruch; Joakim is the other possible subject.
b: The Greek runs on from 1:7: "to Joakim ... when he took the vessels". The pronoun could point back to Joakim, the last man named, or to Baruch, the main figure of the frame. Most English versions, like the Plain, take it as Baruch, who carries the gifts and the vessels to Jerusalem; the KJV has "when he received". The verb lambanō means both "take" and "receive". If Joakim is meant, the verse dates the gift to the day the vessels reached the priest in Jerusalem.
orig: ἐν τῷ λαβεῖν αὐτόν (en tō labein auton), 'when he took'

a: They were silver vessels, made by Zedekiah son of Josiah
p: No other ancient text speaks of silver vessels made by Zedekiah or of their return before Cyrus.
b: Kings says Nebuchadnezzar hauled out the treasures of the LORD's house in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:13) and broke up the bronze in 586 (2 Kings 25:13). Jeremiah told the priests that the objects would not come back soon (Jeremiah 27:16) but would stay in Babylon "until the day I call for them" (Jeremiah 27:22); a false prophet promised them within two years (Jeremiah 28:3). Ezra says Cyrus gave the vessels back (Ezra 1:7). Baruch's silver vessels made by Zedekiah, perhaps to replace those taken in 597, are known from this verse only. Toy called it a "singular historical statement" that points to a writer living long after the events. Readers who hold the frame as history read it as a smaller, earlier return of new vessels that the other books do not record.
r: 2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13; Jeremiah 27:16; Jeremiah 27:22; Jeremiah 28:3; Ezra 1:7

a: the tenth day of Sivan
p: Sivan is the third month of the Jewish year, in late spring.
b: The Greek Seiouan is the Babylonian and later Jewish month name Sivan, the third month, as in Esther 8:9 ("the third month, Sivan"). Codex Alexandrinus spells it Iouan, a slip that drops the first letter. Month names taken from Babylon, such as Sivan and Kislev, appear only in books written during and after the exile (Esther, Nehemiah, Zechariah), and that fits the frame's setting in Babylon.
orig: Σειουάν (Seiouan), Sivan

a: Make grain offerings
p: The Greek says "make manna". It is a Hebrew word for the grain offering, written in Greek letters.
b: The Greek has poiēsate manna, "make manna", and the KJV keeps "prepare ye manna". This is not the food from heaven of the wilderness. The Hebrew word for the grain offering, minchah, was sometimes written in Greek letters instead of translated: the Greek of Jeremiah does the same, listing "burnt offerings and sacrifice ... and manna and frankincense" where the Hebrew has "grain offering" (Jeremiah 17:26; compare Jeremiah 41:5). Toy took the word as a sign that Baruch's first part was translated from Hebrew. The Douay, from the Latin, has "meat offerings", the old English sense of "meat" as food.
orig: μάννα (manna), for Hebrew מִנְחָה (minchah), 'grain offering'

a: bring them up to the altar of the Lord our God
p: The exiles send money for sacrifices in Jerusalem after the temple was burned. Jeremiah 41:5 shows such worship.
b: Agrees: Deuteronomy allows sacrifice only at the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:5), and the exiles send their gifts there rather than offering in Babylon. Jeremiah tells of eighty men who came after the city's fall with "grain offerings and frankincense in their hands to bring to the house of the LORD" (Jeremiah 41:5), so worship at the ruined site did go on. Goes beyond: no book of the 66 speaks of a working altar and priests in Jerusalem five years after the burning, with an exile community paying for whole burnt offerings and sin offerings. The scene looks more like the temple of the writer's own day than the ruins of 581 BC, and critical readers take it as a sign of a later date.

a: pray that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon may live
p: Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon. The Persian decree and Paul ask the same for kings.
b: Jeremiah wrote to the exiles: "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD" (Jeremiah 29:7). Darius' decree for the rebuilt temple asks the priests to "pray for the life of the king and of his sons" (Ezra 6:10), the same pairing as here. Paul asks churches to pray "for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:2). The request is striking because Nebuchadnezzar is the king who burned Jerusalem (1:2). The exiles accept the prophets' word that serving Babylon is God's will for this time (2:21).

a: his son Belshazzar
p: Baruch, like Daniel 5, calls Belshazzar Nebuchadnezzar's son. Babylonian texts make him Nabonidus's son.
b: Daniel 5 calls Nebuchadnezzar "his father" (Daniel 5:2) and Belshazzar "his son" (Daniel 5:22). Babylonian records name Bel-shar-usur as the son of Nabonidus, the last king (see the topic page). Baruch follows Daniel's picture. Toy mentions writers of his day who saw the two princes as stand-ins for the Roman emperor Vespasian and his son Titus, which would date the book after AD 70; he did not decide the question. Those who hold the book as Scripture answer the problem as they answer it in Daniel 5, where "father" and "son" can mean ancestor and successor.

a: so that they last on earth as long as the sky does
p: The Greek says "that their days may be as the days of heaven on the earth": a Hebrew way of saying forever.
b: The phrase is the Greek form of a Hebrew idiom. Deuteronomy promises Israel days on the land "as many as the days the sky is above the earth" (Deuteronomy 11:21), and a psalm promises David's line a throne "for as many days as the heavens have" (Psalm 89:29). Using a blessing like this for the Babylonian kings shows how fully the exiles accept their rule for now.
orig: ὡς αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (hōs hai hēmerai tou ouranou epi tēs gēs)

a: We will live in the shade of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
p: Shade is a picture of a king's protection. Lamentations used it of Judah's own king.
b: In the ancient Near East a king was pictured as a shade tree or a shelter under which his people live. Lamentations says of Judah's anointed king: "In his shade we will live among the nations" (Lamentations 4:20). Baruch's exiles now say the same of the Babylonian king. Jeremiah promised that the nation that "serves him" would stay on its land (Jeremiah 27:11). The verse sounds the book's message for exiles: accept foreign rule as God's discipline, and wait for God's rescue (4:21–24).

a: make confession with it in the Lord's house
t: A confession to be read in public
p: The book is sent to be read aloud at the temple on feast days. One ancient source says Jews read it in the summer.
b: The confession that follows (1:15–3:8) is meant for public worship, read aloud "on the day of the feast and on the days of its season". Gigot saw this as a sign that the book was first written in Hebrew, the language of temple worship. The Apostolic Constitutions, a Christian church order of the late 300s, say that Jews "on the tenth day of the month Gorpiaeus" read "the Lamentations of Jeremiah" and Baruch. Toy thought Gorpiaeus here was probably the month of Av, the month of mourning for the temple, but he doubted the report; if true, it would show the custom of some Greek-speaking Jews only. No Jewish source confirms it.

a: Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but to us belongs the shame of our faces
p: From here to 2:19 Baruch follows Daniel's prayer phrase by phrase, adding more and moving parts around.
b: Compare Daniel 9:7: "Righteousness belongs to you, Lord, but to us belongs the shame of our faces, as it is today: to the people of Judah, to the people living in Jerusalem". The Plain keeps the site's Daniel wording wherever the Greek of Baruch matches the Greek of Daniel, so the reader can see the borrowing. One difference runs through: Daniel's Hebrew has the divine name YHWH, "the LORD", while Baruch's Greek has kyrios, "the Lord". Gigot noted that this section "has much in common" with Daniel 9:4–19. Toy judged that Baruch "most naturally" borrows from Daniel, and thought the reverse, or a common source, less likely. If Baruch borrows, it was written after Daniel, whose final form most scholars date about 165 BC. Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and the Prayer of Azariah are prayers of the same kind.

a: to our priests and our prophets
p: Daniel 9:8 names kings, officials and ancestors. Baruch adds the priests and the prophets.
b: Daniel confesses for "our kings, our officials and our ancestors" (Daniel 9:8). Baruch adds priests and prophets, the two groups Jeremiah blamed most (Jeremiah 23:11), and whose bones Jeremiah saw brought out of their graves (Jeremiah 8:1). The list, with its repeated "our", makes the point that no one in the nation stands outside the confession, including the religious leaders.

a: to walk by the Lord's commands
p: Baruch uses three Greek words for God's law. The Plain gives each one its own English word.
b: Prostagmata, "commands" or "decrees" (1:18; 2:10; 4:1), is the word Baruch uses where Daniel's Greek has "laws" (Daniel 9:10). Entolai, "commandments" (3:9; 4:13), and dikaiōmata, "rulings" (2:12; 4:13), are the other two. In 2:19 dikaiōmata has its other meaning, "righteous deeds". Keeping the words apart lets the reader see that the poem's "book of the commands of God" (4:1) uses the same word as the confession.
orig: πορεύεσθαι τοῖς προστάγμασιν Κυρίου (poreuesthai tois prostagmasin Kyriou)

a: We have carelessly refused to listen to his voice
p: The Greek verb means to act offhand, without thought. The KJV says "negligent"; the Latin says "going astray".
b: Schediazō means to do something on the spur of the moment, carelessly, as a sketch is thrown together. The exiles confess not open defiance only but a long habit of not paying attention: "we were careless toward not hearing his voice". The KJV has "we have been negligent in not hearing his voice"; the Latin, behind the Douay, has "going astray we turned away from hearing his voice". The word is rare in the Greek Bible.
orig: ἐσχεδιάζομεν (eschediazomen), 'we acted offhand'

a: the curse that the Lord laid on Moses his servant
p: The disasters are the curses Moses wrote down. Daniel 9:11 says the same in almost the same words.
b: Deuteronomy warns, "if you will not listen to the LORD your God ... then all these curses will come on you and catch up with you" (Deuteronomy 28:15). Daniel says "the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, were poured out on us" (Daniel 9:11). Baruch says they "clung to us", a picture repeated in 3:4. The confession reads the exile as the covenant working as Moses said it would: God has kept his word, both promise and warning.

a: against our judges who judged Israel
p: This verse follows Daniel 9:12 closely. Some Greek copies add the next words of Daniel too.
b: Daniel 9:12: "He has carried out the word he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us, bringing a great disaster on us." Baruch says "who judged Israel" and adds kings, officials, and the people of Israel and Judah. Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Marchalianus and a later palimpsest also add Daniel's "bringing great disasters on us" (see the variant on this verse). The addition makes Baruch match Daniel even more closely. The shorter text of Codex Vaticanus is followed here.

a: men among us would eat the flesh of their own sons
p: Moses warned that a siege would drive people to eat their children. Lamentations says it happened.
b: The law of Moses has the warning: "You will eat the flesh of your sons" (Leviticus 26:29), and "you will eat your own children, the flesh of the sons and daughters the LORD your God gave you" (Deuteronomy 28:53). Kings tells of it in Samaria's siege (2 Kings 6:28–29), and Lamentations of Jerusalem's: "Women known for compassion boiled their own children" (Lamentations 4:10). The confession names the most terrible of the curses to show that God's word came true to the letter (2:2), and so his promises will too (2:34–35).

a: a disgrace and a waste among all the peoples
p: Deuteronomy warned that scattered Israel would become a shocking sight and a joke among the peoples.
b: Moses warned: "You will become a sight that shocks people, an example in their sayings and a target of their jokes, among all the peoples the LORD drives you to" (Deuteronomy 28:37). The Greek abaton, "a place no one walks through", is the waste land of a ruined country; Baruch uses it again for the land in 2:23. The verse shifts from "us" to "them" and back, a feature of the Hebrew prayer style that the Greek keeps.

a: They ended up underneath and not on top
p: The Greek reverses Deuteronomy's blessing: Israel would be on top, not underneath.
b: Deuteronomy promised that the LORD would make Israel "the head and not the tail. You will only rise and never sink" if they listened (Deuteronomy 28:13), and warned that for the disobedient the foreigner "will be the head, and you the tail" (Deuteronomy 28:44). Baruch's Greek, "they became below and not above", is the same reversal. The confession again reads Israel's state as the covenant's warning come true.
orig: ὑποκάτω καὶ οὐκ ἐπάνω (hypokatō kai ouk epanō), 'below and not above'

a: try to win the Lord over
p: The Greek says "we did not entreat the face of the Lord", the phrase of Daniel 9:13 in its Greek form.
b: The Greek edeēthēmen tou prosōpou Kyriou is word for word the Greek of Daniel 9:13, which translates a Hebrew idiom, literally "to soften the face" of someone, that is, to plead with him and win him over. The Plain uses the site's wording from Daniel 9:13, "we did not try to win the LORD our God over". Baruch fills in what turning back means: each person turning "from the plans of our wicked hearts", the phrase of 1:22.
orig: οὐκ ἐδεήθημεν τοῦ προσώπου Κυρίου (ouk edeēthēmen tou prosōpou Kyriou)

a: The Lord kept watch over the disasters
p: As in Daniel 9:14, God "kept watch" over the disaster: he did not forget what he had said.
b: The verb grēgoreō, "stay awake, keep watch", is the one Daniel 9:14 uses in Greek. It recalls Jeremiah's first vision, an almond branch, with God's pun: "I am watching over my word to do it" (Jeremiah 1:12). The confession ends this section with the reason: "the Lord is in the right". God's justice, not his weakness, explains the fall of Jerusalem.

a: a raised arm
p: Hebrew speaks of God's "outstretched arm" at the Exodus. Baruch's Greek says "a high arm".
b: Deuteronomy says "The LORD brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, with signs and with wonders" (Deuteronomy 26:8). Baruch's list matches it, but the Greek brachioni hypsēlō means "with a high arm", an arm lifted to strike. The Plain keeps the Greek picture. The list adds to Daniel 9:15, which names only the strong hand.
orig: ἐν βραχίονι ὑψηλῷ (en brachioni hypsēlō), 'with a high arm'

a: We have sinned. We have acted wickedly. We have done wrong
p: Three verbs for sin: the confession Solomon taught for exiles to pray in a foreign land.
b: Solomon's prayer at the temple foresaw exiles who, "in their captors' land", would say: "We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil" (1 Kings 8:47). A psalm uses the same three (Psalm 106:6), and Daniel's prayer begins with a longer list (Daniel 9:5). Baruch's exiles say the words Solomon put in their mouths, as if to claim the promise that God would hear them from heaven (1 Kings 8:49–50).

a: your name is called over Israel
p: A Hebrew way of saying "Israel belongs to you", as in Daniel 9:18-19.
b: In Hebrew, to have someone's name "called over" a thing is to be his property: a city, a temple or a people. Daniel ends his prayer with "your name is called over your city and your people" (Daniel 9:19). Baruch uses it of Israel and of the temple (2:26). The plea is that God's own reputation is bound up with his people, so that rescuing them shows the whole earth who he is.
orig: τὸ ὄνομά σου ἐπεκλήθη ἐπὶ Ἰσραήλ (to onoma sou epeklēthē epi Israēl)

a: look down from your holy house
p: The words follow the prayer of Deuteronomy 26:15 and Daniel 9:18.
b: Deuteronomy gives the farmer a prayer: "Look down from your holy dwelling, from the heavens, and bless your people Israel" (Deuteronomy 26:15). Daniel prays "bend your ear and listen. Open your eyes and look" (Daniel 9:18). Baruch joins the two. With the temple in Jerusalem burned, God's "holy house" is heaven.

a: It is not the dead in Hades
t: The dead do not praise God
p: The exiles argue that only the living can praise God, as several psalms do. 3:4 seems to say otherwise.
b: Agrees: the plea is an old one in Israel's prayers: "among the dead no one calls you to mind. In Sheol, who gives you thanks?" (Psalm 6:5); "The dead do not praise Yah" (Psalm 115:17); "It is not Sheol that thanks you ... The living, the living: they are the ones who thank you" (Isaiah 38:18–19). Hades is the Greek word for Sheol, the place of the dead. The argument is: keep us alive, and we will praise you. Tension: a few verses on, the same prayer asks God to hear "the prayer of the dead of Israel" (3:4). The note there gives the likely explanation. Later Jewish and Christian teaching about the dead with God is weighed in the topic pages.

a: whose spirit was taken from within them
p: The Greek speaks of the spirit taken from the "inner parts". The Douay says "bowels".
b: Pneuma, "spirit" or "breath", is the life God gives and takes back (Psalm 104:29; Ecclesiastes 12:7). Splanchna are the inner organs, which Greek used for the seat of feeling. The phrase pictures death as the breath of life leaving the body. The KJV has "whose souls are taken from their bodies", which reads later ideas of the soul into the line.
orig: ὧν ἐλήμφθη τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῶν ἀπὸ τῶν σπλάγχνων αὐτῶν (hōn elēmphthē to pneuma autōn apo tōn splanchnōn autōn)

a: the soul crushed by grief
p: The Greek says the soul grieves "over the greatness" and does not say of what. The Latin adds "of evil".
b: The Greek reads "the soul that grieves over the greatness", which is hard to follow. It may mean grief beyond measure, which is how the KJV takes it ("greatly vexed") and the Plain. The Latin fills the gap, "sorrowful for the greatness of evil", and the Douay adds "she hath done".
orig: ἡ λυπουμένη ἐπὶ τὸ μέγεθος (hē lypoumenē epi to megethos)

a: on the strength of what our ancestors and our kings did right
p: Like Daniel 9:18, the plea rests on God's compassion, not on anyone's good deeds.
b: Agrees: Daniel prays, "We are not laying our pleas in front of you because of our righteous deeds, but because of your great compassion" (Daniel 9:18), and Moses told Israel "it is not because you are righteous" that they received the land (Deuteronomy 9:6). Baruch rules out even the good deeds of the ancestors and the kings, the merit of others, and grounds the plea on God's gentleness and compassion (2:27). Christian readers of every tradition have found here the same basis for prayer that the New Testament teaches.

a: Bow your shoulder and work for the king of Babylon
p: The prophets' message here is Jeremiah's: put your neck under Babylon's yoke and live.
b: Jeremiah told Zedekiah: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon ... Serve him and his people, and live" (Jeremiah 27:12), and promised that the nation that serves him would stay on its land (Jeremiah 27:11). The Greek of Jeremiah has "neck" and "work for the king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 34:9–10 in the Greek order); Baruch keeps "work for the king of Babylon" but says "bow your shoulder". The confession quotes the prophet's warning to admit that the people refused it (2:24).

a: the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
p: Jeremiah's repeated threat, and his promise that the songs would be heard again.
b: Jeremiah says it four times: "I will put a stop to the sound of joy and the sound of gladness, the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride" (Jeremiah 7:34; compare Jeremiah 16:9; Jeremiah 25:10). The fourth time it is a promise: the same sounds will "again" be heard in the ruined towns (Jeremiah 33:10–11). Baruch quotes the threat, and the second half of the book moves toward the promise, ending with Jerusalem's children coming home in gladness (5:9).

a: the bones of our kings and the bones of our ancestors
p: Jeremiah foretold that the bones of Judah's kings and leaders would be brought out of their graves.
b: "At that time, the LORD declares, they will bring out of their graves the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its officials, the bones of the priests" (Jeremiah 8:1), to lie spread out under the sky (Jeremiah 8:2). To be left unburied was a great disgrace in Israel. The exiles say this word too has come true.

a: the heat of the day and the frost of the night
p: Jeremiah said King Jehoiakim's body would lie exposed to heat by day and frost by night.
b: The phrase is Jeremiah's word against King Jehoiakim: "His corpse will be flung out into the heat of the day and the frost of the night" (Jeremiah 36:30). Baruch widens it to the bones of all the kings and ancestors (2:24). Jehoiakim was the king who burned the scroll that Baruch wrote (Jeremiah 36:23, 32), so the echo fits a book in Baruch's name.

a: banishment
p: The Greek says "sending away". The KJV says "pestilence", the Douay "banishment".
b: The third of Jeremiah's usual three is sword, famine and disease (Jeremiah 32:36). Baruch's Greek has apostolē, "sending away". The Greek of Jeremiah has the same word in the same verse (Jeremiah 39:36 in the Greek numbering, which is Jeremiah 32:36 in the Hebrew), where the Hebrew has dever, "disease". Why the Greek has this word is not clear, but Baruch agrees with the Greek of Jeremiah. The KJV, translating the sense, gives "pestilence"; the Latin and the Douay keep "banishment". The Plain follows the Greek.
orig: ἐν ἀποστολῇ (en apostolē), 'in sending away'

a: you have made the house over which your name is called what it is today
p: Most read the temple's ruin in 586 BC. Some scholars have read the temple's ruin in AD 70.
b: The frame sets the book after the Babylonians burned the temple (1:2), and on that reading the house is Solomon's temple in ruins. Toy reports that Kneucker and others dated parts of Baruch after the Romans destroyed the second temple in AD 70, while Kneucker himself allowed an earlier, Maccabean date if the first part of this verse was added later. Both readings take the confession as a prayer for a people whose temple lies in ruins. On either view the prayer works the same way for its readers: it explains a national disaster as the covenant's discipline and asks for God's compassion (2:27).

a: as you spoke through your servant Moses
t: A promise of Moses in new words
p: The words given to Moses in 2:29-35 are not found in this form in the law. They gather Deuteronomy and Jeremiah.
b: Agrees: the promise is built from Moses' own words: only a handful would be left (Deuteronomy 28:62); in exile they would "take them to heart" (Deuteronomy 30:1) and God would gather them back (Deuteronomy 30:3) and circumcise their hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6); Leviticus promises that God will not break his covenant even in the land of their enemies (Leviticus 26:44). Goes beyond: the closing promise of an everlasting covenant (2:35) comes from Jeremiah (Jeremiah 32:40), not from the law. Baruch puts the whole in Moses' mouth, treating the prophets' promises as part of what God told Moses would happen. This is a free summary, as Jewish prayers of the period often made, not a quotation.

a: this great swarm of people
p: The Greek word means a humming or buzzing, used for a huge crowd. It is rare in the Greek Bible.
b: Bombēsis is the hum of bees or the roar of a crowd. Moses said Israel was "once as many as the stars in the sky" but "only a handful of you will be left" (Deuteronomy 28:62). The Plain says "swarm" to keep the sound of a crowd too big to count.
orig: ἡ βόμβησις ἡ μεγάλη ἡ πολλὴ αὕτη (hē bombēsis hē megalē hē pollē hautē)

a: they will come to their senses
p: The Greek says "they will turn to their heart", Moses' phrase for exiles who take God's word to heart.
b: The Hebrew idiom behind the Greek is the one in Deuteronomy 30:1, "you will take them to heart", and in Solomon's prayer, "if, in the land where they were taken as prisoners, they take it to heart and turn back" (1 Kings 8:47). The Plain says "come to their senses" because the idiom means a change of mind, not a feeling. God speaks of it as certain: the same exile that punishes them will be where they repent.
orig: ἐπιστρέψουσιν ἐπὶ καρδίαν αὐτῶν (epistrepsousin epi kardian autōn)

a: they are a stiff-necked people
p: Moses' word for Israel, used again in 2:33 ("their stubbornness", literally "their hard back").
b: "You are a stiff-necked people" (Deuteronomy 9:6); "I know your defiance and your stiff neck" (Deuteronomy 31:27). The picture is of an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke. Baruch carries it on in 2:33, where the Greek says they will turn back "from their hard back", and in 2:21, where the prophet tells them to bow the shoulder.

a: I will give them a heart and ears that listen
p: The promise of a heart that listens joins Deuteronomy 30, Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
b: Moses promised that God would "circumcise your heart" (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah: "I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD" (Jeremiah 24:7). Ezekiel: "I will give you a new heart" (Ezekiel 36:26). Baruch adds ears, because the sin confessed again and again is that they "did not listen to the voice" (1:18, 1:21, 2:5). The cure matches the sickness.

a: an everlasting covenant
p: The promise comes from Jeremiah 32:40, with the old covenant words "I will be God to them".
b: Jeremiah: "I will cut an everlasting covenant with them" (Jeremiah 32:40), and "They will become my people, and I will become their God" (Jeremiah 32:38; compare Jeremiah 31:33). The last line, "I will never again move my people Israel out of the land", goes past Jeremiah's words. Jewish readers have read it as God's lasting promise of the land; many Christian readers have read the everlasting covenant in the light of the new covenant of Jeremiah 31, which the New Testament says is made in Christ (Hebrews 8:8–12).

a: Lord Almighty, God of Israel
p: Greek pantokratōr, "ruler of all", the Greek Bible's usual word for the Hebrew "LORD of Armies".
b: The title opens the last part of the confession (3:1–8) and returns in 3:4. Pantokratōr is the word the Greek translators often used for the Hebrew tseva'ot, "of Armies", in the title "the LORD of Armies", and it is the word of Revelation's "the Lord God, the Almighty" (Revelation 4:8). The prayer calls on God's power over all things just when the people feel most powerless: "a soul hemmed in".
orig: Κύριε Παντοκράτωρ (Kyrie Pantokratōr)

a: You are seated on your throne for all time
p: The contrast of Lamentations 5:19-20: God reigns forever, so why are we forgotten?
b: "You, LORD, sit as king forever; your throne lasts from generation to generation. Why do you keep forgetting us?" (Lamentations 5:19–20). Baruch makes the contrast sharper with the same phrase on both sides: God is seated "for all time", and we perish "for all time". The Latin turns the second half into a question, "and shall we perish everlastingly?", which the Douay follows.

a: the prayer of the dead of Israel
p: The Greek says "the dead of Israel", which clashes with 2:17. A misread Hebrew word may lie behind it.
b: In 2:17 the prayer says the dead cannot praise God; here it asks him to hear "the prayer of the dead of Israel". The UBS translators' handbook by Bullard and Hatton explains that the Hebrew for "dead" is spelled like a rare word for "men", used of a small number of people in Genesis 34:30 and Deuteronomy 26:5. In Hebrew without vowel marks, metei Yisra'el can be read either way, and the very phrase "men of Israel" stands in Isaiah 41:14, which the site renders "you small band of Israel". The Greek translator may have read "dead", perhaps led by the dead of 2:17. The handbook notes Moore's "the men of Israel" and the New American Bible's "the few". Others keep "dead" and read it as exiles who are as good as dead (3:10–11). The Plain follows the Greek.
orig: τῶν τεθνηκότων Ἰσραήλ (tōn tethnēkotōn Israēl), 'of the dead of Israel'; Hebrew מְתֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (metei Yisra'el) 'men of Israel' (Isaiah 41:14)

a: call to mind your hand and your name
p: "Hand" is God's power, the power that brought Israel out of Egypt (2:11).
b: The Greek is literally "remember your hand and your name". In Hebrew speech the hand is power in action, and the confession has already recalled "a strong hand" at the Exodus (2:11). The prayer asks God to remember, not the sins of the past, but his own power and his reputation. The Plain keeps "hand" so the link with 2:11 stays visible.
orig: μνήσθητι χειρός σου καὶ ὀνόματός σου (mnēsthēti cheiros sou kai onomatos sou)

a: a debt to be paid
p: The Greek word means a debt or a fine owed. The KJV says "subject to payments".
b: Ophlēsis is a legal and business word: something owed, a penalty to be paid. The prayer pictures the ancestors' sins as a debt the exiles are still paying off. Isaiah uses a similar picture for the end of the exile: "her guilt has been paid off" (Isaiah 40:2). The confession ends on this low note, "who walked away from the Lord our God", and the poem that follows answers it with a call to come back.
orig: ὄφλησις (ophlēsis), 'debt, penalty'

a: Listen, Israel, to the commandments of life
p: The poem opens with the first words of the Shema, and with Moses' call to choose life.
b: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4) is Israel's daily confession of faith, the Shema. The poem on wisdom (3:9–4:4) begins with the same two words, and it ends with Israel's happiness at knowing what pleases God (4:4). "Commandments of life" recalls Moses' last appeal: "Life and death are what I have put before you ... Choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). The confession had looked back on failure; the poem turns to what Israel should do now.

a: learn insight
p: The poem uses four Greek words: wisdom, insight, understanding, discernment. The Plain keeps them apart.
b: Sophia is "wisdom" (3:12, 3:23); phronēsis, practical good judgment, is "insight" (3:9, 3:14, 3:28); epistēmē, knowledge, is "understanding" (3:20, 3:27, 3:37); and synesis, the power to put things together, is "discernment" (3:14, 3:23, 3:32). The poem treats them as one thing seen from different sides, and from 3:15 on speaks of it as "she", like Lady Wisdom in Proverbs (Proverbs 1:20; Proverbs 8:1).
orig: φρόνησις (phronēsis), 'insight'; σοφία (sophia), 'wisdom'; ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē), 'understanding'; σύνεσις (synesis), 'discernment'

a: made unclean with the dead
p: The poet pictures exile as living among the dead and already counted as going down to Hades.
b: A foreign land was unclean ground for Israel, and contact with the dead made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11). The poet stacks the images: grown old in a strange land, unclean with the dead, counted with those who go down to Hades. Exile is a living death. The same picture explains "the prayer of the dead of Israel" in 3:4 on one reading, and it prepares for Ezekiel's vision of dry bones, where God tells the prophet "the whole house of Israel is these bones" (Ezekiel 37:11).

a: You abandoned the spring of wisdom
p: Jeremiah's charge: Israel left God, "the spring of living water". Here the spring is wisdom.
b: "My people have done two wrongs: me they have left, the spring of living water, to dig themselves cisterns ... that do not hold the water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Baruch gives the reason for the exile as a single line: Israel left the source of wisdom. The next verse states the other side: walking in God's way would have meant peace forever (3:13).

a: Who has found where she lives?
p: The poem asks Job 28's question, where wisdom can be found, and gives the same answer: only God knows.
b: "But wisdom: where can it be found? Where does understanding have its home?" (Job 28:12). Job answers that it cannot be bought (Job 28:15), "God has the insight into its road" (Job 28:23), and to humans he gives the fear of the Lord (Job 28:28). Baruch follows the same path: rulers and merchants could not find her (3:16–23), giants could not (3:26–28), no one climbed to heaven for her (3:29–30), but God knows her (3:32) and gave her to Israel (3:37). Gigot pointed to Job 28 and Job 38 as the poem's models.

a: Where are the rulers of the nations now
p: A classic lament: the great of the earth, their hunts and their treasures, are gone.
b: The poem uses the old question "where are they?" to show that power and wealth do not lead to wisdom. Ancient kings boasted of mastering wild beasts and birds, and the hunt was a royal sport across the Near East; the poet's rulers are "masters of the wild animals" who "played with the birds of the sky" and piled up silver and gold. All of them "went down to Hades" (3:19). The theme is common in the wisdom books (Psalm 49:10–17; Ecclesiastes 2:4–11). In Daniel, God gave Nebuchadnezzar rule over the beasts and birds (Daniel 2:38), so the first readers may have heard a hint of Babylon's kings.

a: no one saw her in Teman
t: The famous wise men of Teman
p: Teman in Edom was known for its wise men. Job's friend Eliphaz came from there.
b: Jeremiah asks about Edom, "Is wisdom finished in Teman?" (Jeremiah 49:7), and Obadiah has God "destroy the wise from Edom" (Obadiah 8). Job's first comforter is "Eliphaz the Temanite" (Job 2:11). Canaan stands for the coast of Phoenicia, a land of traders. The poet names the peoples most admired for worldly wisdom and trade, and says none of them found her.

a: The descendants of Hagar
t: Hagar's sons, Merran and the storytellers
p: The Arab traders descended from Ishmael, a place called Merran, and the tellers of tales.
b: "The sons of Hagar" are the Ishmaelite tribes of the desert, known as caravan traders: Joseph's brothers sold him to "a line of Ishmaelite traders" (Genesis 37:25). Merran is not known from any other text; the Latin has Merrha. The Greek mythologoi, "tellers of stories", may mean people who passed on proverbs and fables, the wisdom of the nations. All are "searchers for discernment", and the poet grants that they search seriously, but they did not find the way.
orig: οἱ υἱοὶ Ἁγάρ (hoi huioi Hagar); οἱ μυθολόγοι (hoi mythologoi), 'the storytellers'

a: how great God's house is
p: Here "God's house" is the universe, not the temple: wide, endless, high and beyond measure.
b: Elsewhere in Baruch the Lord's house is the temple in Jerusalem (1:8, 1:14). In the poem the next lines show that the "house" is God's whole creation, "great and without end". The Greek ktēsis, "possession", is the same word used in 3:17 for the rulers' getting and gaining; their wealth had no end, but God's estate is the whole world. The giants were "born there", that is, on the earth (3:26).
orig: ὁ οἶκος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho oikos tou theou)

a: There the giants were born
p: The poet means the giants of Genesis 6:4, the "men with a name" of the earliest days.
b: In Greek, Genesis 6:4 calls the Nephilim hoi gigantes, "the giants", and ends with "the giants who were from the age, the famous men" (Swete's text). Baruch's "famous from the beginning" echoes it closely. The site's Plain of Genesis 6:4, from the Hebrew, says "the heroes of ancient times, men with a name". Jewish writers of this period told much more about the giants, as in 1 Enoch; Baruch makes only one point: size and skill at war did not bring wisdom, and "they died out". The Wisdom of Solomon tells of "the proud giants" dying in the Flood (Wisdom 14:6).
orig: οἱ γίγαντες οἱ ὀνομαστοὶ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς (hoi gigantes hoi onomastoi ap' archēs)

a: Who has climbed up into the sky and taken her
t: Up to the sky, across the sea
p: Baruch reuses Moses' words about the law being near, and Paul reuses them for Christ.
b: Moses said of the commandment: "It is not in the sky, so that you would ask, 'Who will climb up into the sky for us and get it ...?'" and "It is not on the far side of the sea" (Deuteronomy 30:12–13). Baruch asks the same two questions of wisdom (3:29–30) and answers, like Moses, that God has brought her near to Israel as the law (3:37–4:1). Paul quotes Deuteronomy's lines and applies them to Christ: "'Who will go up into heaven?' (That is, to bring Christ down.)" (Romans 10:6). Paul quotes Deuteronomy, not Baruch, but both show that Jews of the time read Deuteronomy 30 as being about the word or wisdom that God brings down to people. John has Jesus say that "nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven" (John 3:13).

a: will bring her back for choice gold
p: No one can buy wisdom, Job and Proverbs say. The poet's merchants (3:23) never found her.
b: "No fine gold can be handed over for it" (Job 28:15); "wisdom is better than red coral" (Proverbs 8:11). The Greek can mean "bring her for choice gold", as a trader carries goods home from across the sea; the rich of 3:17 who trusted in gold are answered here.

a: the one who knows everything knows her
p: As in Job 28:23-24, the creator who sees the whole earth is the one who knows where wisdom is.
b: "God has the insight into its road; he is the one who knows its whereabouts. For his gaze reaches the ends of the earth" (Job 28:23–24). Baruch moves straight from God's knowledge to God's work of creation: the earth made ready for ages and filled with animals, then light and stars (3:33–35). Wisdom is found by the one who made the world, and he gives her to whom he chooses (3:37).

a: He sends the light out, and off it goes
p: Job 38:35 asks who can send lightning "and off it goes", saying "Here we are". Baruch splits the picture.
b: God asks Job: "Will you send off the lightning, and off it goes, saying to you, 'Here we are'?" (Job 38:35). Baruch gives the first half to the light, which goes when sent and comes trembling when called, and the answer "Here we are!" to the stars (3:35). Isaiah says God "marches their army out by count and calls each one by name" (Isaiah 40:26), and at creation "the stars of morning sang as one" (Job 38:7). Creation obeys gladly; Israel, the poem implies, should too.

a: each at its post
p: The Greek says the stars shone "in their watches", like sentries at their posts through the night.
b: Phylakai are the watches of the night or the posts where guards stand. The stars are pictured as an army on duty, each in its place, glad to serve the one who made them (3:35). Isaiah and the Psalms speak of the stars as God's army in the same way (Isaiah 40:26).
orig: ἐν ταῖς φυλακαῖς αὐτῶν (en tais phylakais autōn)

a: This is our God
t: "This is our God" in the early church
p: Christians read 3:36-38 of Christ: Cyprian, Hippolytus, the Apostolic Constitutions, and the Orthodox Christmas services.
b: The Hebrew Bible says the same of the LORD: "Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35; compare Isaiah 45:21). Early Christian writers read 3:36–38 together as a prophecy of God come in the flesh. Cyprian of Carthage, in his Testimonies (book 2, section 6, "That Christ is God"), quotes the three verses as from "Jeremiah". Hippolytus of Rome reports that the followers of Noetus used "This is our God" to argue that there is only one divine person, so that the Father himself appeared on earth and suffered; Hippolytus answers that 3:38 speaks of the Son, who received all knowledge from the Father. The Apostolic Constitutions (5.20) quote the lines as foretelling Christ. The Orthodox Church reads 3:36–4:4 at Vespers on Christmas Eve.

a: gave it to his servant Jacob, / to Israel, loved by him
p: The wisdom no nation found, God gave to Israel. Psalm 147 and Deuteronomy 4 say the same of the law.
b: "He tells his words to Jacob, his rules and his rulings to Israel. No other nation has he treated like this" (Psalm 147:19–20). Moses said that keeping the law "will show your wisdom and your understanding to the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:6). Sirach 24 tells the same story: Wisdom sought a home among all peoples and was told by the Creator to settle in Jacob, and then she is named as the book of the covenant, the law of Moses (Sirach 24:8, 23). Baruch makes the same move in 4:1. "Jacob my servant" is Isaiah's title for the people (Isaiah 44:1–2).

a: After this she was seen on earth
t: Wisdom on earth, or God on earth?
p: Read with 4:1, wisdom came to live among people as the law. Many early Christians read it of the incarnation.
b: The Greek verb has no subject word, so it can mean "she was seen" or "he was seen". Wisdom given as the law: the word for "it" in 3:37 is feminine (the way of understanding), and 4:1 goes on "She is the book of the commands of God". So the verse says that wisdom, given to Israel, appeared and lived among people in the form of the law, as Proverbs has Wisdom say "my delights were with human beings" (Proverbs 8:31). The Plain follows this reading. God seen on earth: the Latin (visus est, masculine) and the KJV ("Afterward did he shew himself upon earth") read "he", God himself, and many early Christian writers read it as foretelling the Son made man (see 3:36). A Christian addition: Crawford Toy, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, judged the verse "undoubtedly a Christian interpolation", added to the book by Christians. Swete's notes show no Greek manuscript without the verse, and the Catholic Church reads 3:9–15 and 3:32–4:4 together at the Easter Vigil.

a: went about among human beings
p: Christians have long set this line beside John 1:14. The words are different, and the link is debated.
b: Compared with the Bible: John says "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). The Greek words are not the same: John has eskēnōsen, "pitched his tent", and Baruch synanestraphē, "lived together with, went about with". John's tent picture is closer to Sirach 24:8, where Wisdom pitches her tent in Jacob. One common reading takes the shared idea, God's wisdom coming to live among people, as Jewish wisdom tradition that John and Baruch both draw on, not a quotation. For Catholic and Orthodox readers, who hold Baruch as Scripture, the verse belongs among the Old Testament witnesses to the incarnation that the Fathers gathered. Protestants, for whom Baruch is not Scripture, read it as a witness to the Jewish background of John 1.
orig: ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις συνανεστράφη (en tois anthrōpois synanestraphē)

a: She is the book of the commands of God
p: The poem names the hidden wisdom: it is the law of Moses, the book Israel already has.
b: Here the poem reaches its answer. The wisdom that the nations, the rich and the giants could not find is "the book of the commands of God, the law that lasts forever". Sirach says the same: "All this is the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses commanded us" (Sirach 24:23). Moses had told Israel the law would be their wisdom "to the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:6). Later Jewish teaching built on this, that the Torah was the wisdom God used at creation. For Christians the same title, God's wisdom, belongs to Christ (1 Corinthians 1:24), which is one reason 3:38 was read as it was.

a: Everyone who holds on to her is headed for life
t: Hold on to her and live
p: Proverbs says the same of wisdom: she is a tree of life to those who grab hold of her.
b: "To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life" (Proverbs 3:18); "Grab discipline and never let go. Keep her safe: she is your life" (Proverbs 4:13). The Greek is short and sharp: "all who hold her, to life; those who leave her will die". It is Moses' choice of life and death again (Deuteronomy 30:15), and the reverse of 3:12, where Israel "abandoned" the spring of wisdom.

a: or what benefits you to a foreign nation
p: A warning not to give Israel's treasure, the law, away to others. Readers differ on who the others are.
b: On its face the line warns Israel not to lose its glory, the law (4:1), to the nations by giving up its own way of life. Toy allowed that the "foreign nation" may mean Greek culture, which drew many Jews away in the second century BC, rather than the Christian church, which claimed Israel's Scriptures, as others had read it. Readers who date the poem early see a warning against the pull of Greek ways; readers who date it after AD 70 can hear the rivalry with the church. The verse itself names no one.

a: How happy we are, Israel!
p: The poem ends as Moses' blessing ends: "How happy you are, Israel!"
b: Moses' last blessing closes: "How happy you are, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?" (Deuteronomy 33:29). Moses also asked, "what great nation has rules and rulings as just as this whole law?" (Deuteronomy 4:8). The poem ends on joy, not shame: Israel knows what pleases God, and that is its wealth among the nations.

a: you who keep Israel's name alive
p: The Greek calls the people "the memorial of Israel": those who keep the name Israel alive.
b: Mnēmosynon is something that keeps a memory alive, like a monument. The exiles are what is left of Israel, the remnant that keeps its name from dying out. The KJV and Douay keep "the memorial of Israel". The third part of the book (4:5–5:9) opens here, a poem of comfort, and "Take heart" begins each new stanza (4:5, 4:21, 4:27, 4:30).
orig: μνημόσυνον Ἰσραήλ (mnēmosynon Israēl)

a: You were sold to the nations
p: God "sold" Israel to its enemies as discipline, not to destroy it, as Isaiah and Deuteronomy say.
b: Moses' song: their enemies won "unless their Rock had sold them off and the LORD had given them away" (Deuteronomy 32:30). Isaiah: "it was for your guilt that you were sold" (Isaiah 50:1), and "For nothing you were sold, and not with silver will you be bought back" (Isaiah 52:3). Baruch adds the comfort: not "to be wiped out". The exile is a sale that can be undone.

a: by offering sacrifices to demons and not to God
p: The words of Moses' song. Paul uses the same words for meals in pagan temples.
b: Agrees: Moses' song says "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17), and a psalm says Israel "offered up their own sons and their daughters to demons" (Psalm 106:37). The Greek of Baruch and of Deuteronomy both say daimonia. Paul writes, "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20), the same words, which Paul takes from Deuteronomy. The book's 4:35 brings demons back as the new tenants of the guilty city.

a: You forgot the one who fed you, the everlasting God
t: God the nurse, Jerusalem the mother
p: Moses' song pictures God giving birth to Israel. Baruch gives God the nurse's part and Jerusalem the mother's.
b: "You ignored the Rock who fathered you, and forgot the God who went into labor with you" (Deuteronomy 32:18). Baruch keeps the forgetting and the parent: God "fed" or brought them up, and Jerusalem "nursed" them. The pair sets up the speech that follows, in which Jerusalem herself speaks as a mother who has lost her children (4:9–29).

a: Listen, you who live alongside Zion!
p: The city speaks as a widowed mother, as in Lamentations, to the towns around her.
b: In Lamentations the city weeps like a widow with no one to comfort her (Lamentations 1:1–2) and cries, "My children are ruined" (Lamentations 1:16). Isaiah pictures Zion as a mother who lost her children and gets them back (Isaiah 49:21; Isaiah 54:1). Paul calls "the Jerusalem above" "our mother" (Galatians 4:26). The "neighbors of Zion" are a feminine plural in Greek, probably the towns around Jerusalem, pictured as women: the KJV says "ye that dwell about Sion".
orig: αἱ πάροικοι Σειών (hai paroikoi Seiōn), feminine plural

a: the Everlasting
p: Baruch uses "the Everlasting" by itself as a name for God, in seven verses of chapters 4-5.
b: The Greek ho aiōnios, "the everlasting one", is an adjective used as a name: 4:10, 4:14, 4:20, 4:22 (twice), 4:24, 4:35 and 5:2. The Plain gives it a capital and renders it the same each time. In 4:8 the phrase "the everlasting God" stands in full, as in Genesis 21:33. The title fits a book about a people who feel that they are perishing "for all time" (3:3): their God lasts forever, and so does his gladness (4:29).
orig: ὁ αἰώνιος (ho aiōnios)

a: a widow abandoned by many
p: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a widow. Isaiah turns the image on Babylon, who said she would never be one.
b: "She who was great among the nations has become like a widow" (Lamentations 1:1). Babylon boasted, "I will never sit as a widow or know what it is to lose my children" (Isaiah 47:8), and Isaiah answers that both will come on her "in an instant" (Isaiah 47:9). God promises Zion that "the insults of your widowhood you will remember no more" (Isaiah 54:4). Baruch follows the same turn: the widowed mother here, the city that hurt her grieving in 4:33.

a: the paths of training
p: The Greek paideia is a child's upbringing: training and correction together.
b: Paideia is the word for raising and educating a child, with the correction that goes with it; Proverbs uses it for the "discipline" a father gives (Proverbs 3:11). Codex Vaticanus spells it paidia, which Swete prints; his notes give other spellings from the correctors and from Marchalianus. The mother's complaint fits her picture: she raised children who would not walk the paths of their upbringing.
orig: τρίβους παιδίας (tribous paidias), for παιδείας (paideias), 'training'

a: a nation without shame, speaking a foreign language
p: Moses warned of a nation from far off, speaking an unknown tongue, sparing neither old nor young.
b: "From far off, from the edge of the earth, the LORD will raise up a nation against you ... You will not understand its language. Its people will be grim-faced. They will not honor the old or spare the young" (Deuteronomy 28:49–50). Baruch's mother describes Babylon in Moses' words, again reading the disaster as the covenant's warning come true.

a: the sackcloth of my pleading
p: Sackcloth, rough cloth of goat hair, was worn in mourning and in prayer for mercy.
b: Mourners and people pleading with God put on sackcloth, a coarse, dark cloth, and often sat in ashes (Daniel 9:3; Jonah 3:5–6). The mother takes off "the robe of peace" and puts on mourning dress, and in 5:1 she is told to take off her mourning robe and dress in glory. The clothing marks the turn of the book.

a: the Holy One
p: Baruch calls God "the Holy One" three times (4:22, 4:37, 5:5), as Isaiah calls him "the Holy One of Israel".
b: Ho hagios, "the holy one", is an adjective used as a name, like "the Everlasting" (4:10). Isaiah's favorite title for God is "the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 41:14), and the closing poems of Baruch draw heavily on Isaiah 40–66. The joy that comes to the mother "from the Holy One" is the promise of return.
orig: παρὰ τοῦ ἁγίου (para tou hagiou)

a: over the mercy soon coming to you
p: The Greek eleēmosynē means "almsgiving" for people, but "mercy" when God gives it.
b: In Tobit and Sirach eleēmosynē is the gift to the poor, "alms". Of God, as here and in 5:9, it means his mercy shown in action. Codex Alexandrinus leaves the phrase out, so that the mother's joy is simply "from the Holy One". The mercy, she says, will come "soon" (4:22, 4:24, 4:25): the poem keeps telling the exiles that they will not wait forever.
orig: ἐπὶ τῇ ἐλεημοσύνῃ (epi tē eleēmosynē)

a: put your foot on their necks
p: The victor's foot on the neck of the beaten was a sign of total victory.
b: Joshua told his officers, "Put your feet on the necks of these kings" (Joshua 10:24), and ancient kings were shown in art with their feet on their enemies. Moses' blessing promises that Israel "will tread on their high places" (Deuteronomy 33:29). The mother tells her children that their oppressor will fall "soon". Note the shift from "you" (one people) to "their necks" (the enemies as many).

a: seek him ten times more
p: Turn back with ten times the energy you once put into going astray.
b: Moses promised that in exile "you will search for the LORD your God, and you will find him, when you seek him with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 4:29). The mother's measure, "ten times", matches the effort of repentance to the effort of sin. Jeremiah has the same promise: "You will look for me and find me" (Jeremiah 29:13).

a: the one who gave you your name will comfort you
p: The last part of the book turns to Jerusalem herself with Isaiah's comfort and Isaiah's new name.
b: Isaiah 40 begins "Comfort, comfort my people ... Speak to the heart of Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:1–2). "The one who gave you your name" points ahead to 5:4, where God gives the city a new name, as Isaiah promises: "A new name will be given you, one the LORD's own mouth will pick out" (Isaiah 62:2). From here to 5:9 the poet speaks to Jerusalem as her children once heard her speak to them.

a: miserable is the city that took your sons
p: The city is not named. In the frame it is Babylon; some critics have read it as Rome.
b: The book's frame is in Babylon, and the threats of 4:31–35 follow the oracles against Babylon in Isaiah and Jeremiah closely (Isaiah 13:19–22; Jeremiah 50:39). For the first readers the city stood for any empire that had carried Jews away. Scholars who date the poem after AD 70 have heard in it Rome, which Revelation calls "Babylon the Great" (Revelation 18:2); Toy reports such dates. On any reading the comfort is the same: the empire that took Jerusalem's children will itself be emptied.

a: demons will make her their home
p: The prophets said wild beasts and goat-demons would haunt ruined Babylon. Revelation says the same.
b: Isaiah: "Wild beasts of the desert will lie down there ... and goat-demons will leap about there" (Isaiah 13:21); "Lilith, too, will settle there" (Isaiah 34:14). Jeremiah: "no one will live there, generation after generation" (Jeremiah 50:39). The Greek of Isaiah 13:21 already has daimonia where the Hebrew has the hairy goat-demons. Revelation's angel cries over Babylon: "She has become a home for demons" (Revelation 18:2). Baruch stands between the prophets and Revelation on this road.

a: look around you, toward the sunrise
p: Isaiah's call to the city: raise your eyes and see your children coming home.
b: "Raise your eyes and look around you: they have all gathered; they are coming to you. Your sons arrive from far away" (Isaiah 60:4; compare Isaiah 49:18). The exiles in Babylon lived to the east of Jerusalem, so the city looks toward the sunrise. In 5:5 the call is repeated almost word for word.

a: They come gathered from sunrise to sunset
p: Isaiah's promise that God will gather his people from east and west. Jesus uses the same picture.
b: "From the sunrise I will bring your offspring, and from the sunset I will gather you" (Isaiah 43:5). The gathering is "by the Holy One's word": God's command brings them. Jesus says many "will come from the sunrise and the sunset" to eat with Abraham (Matthew 8:11). The children whom the mother "sent off" with tears (4:11, 4:23) now come back.

a: strip off the robe of your grief and your misery
p: Isaiah's call: Jerusalem, put on your beautiful clothes. The mourning dress of 4:20 comes off.
b: "Wake up, wake up, put on your strength, Zion! Put on your beautiful clothes, Jerusalem, the holy city!" (Isaiah 52:1). "He has wrapped me in a robe of righteousness" (Isaiah 61:10). In 4:20 the mother put on sackcloth; now the poet tells her to take off grief and dress in the glory that comes from God, the cloak of his righteousness and a turban (5:2). The clothes are the city's new standing before the nations.

a: the turban of the glory of the Everlasting
p: The Greek mitra is a headband or turban, a royal and priestly headdress. The cloak is a "double" one.
b: Diplois, the cloak, is a mantle folded double, a large outer garment. Mitra is a headband or turban; Isaiah promises Zion "You will be a beautiful crown in the LORD's hand, a king's turban in the palm of your God" (Isaiah 62:3). Codex Alexandrinus reads "the glory of the Holy One" for "the glory of the Everlasting" (see the variant). The city is dressed as a royal bride or a priest, ready for her children's return.
orig: τὴν διπλοΐδα (tēn diploida), 'the cloak'; τὴν μίτραν (tēn mitran), 'the turban'

a: "Peace of Righteousness" and "Glory of Godliness."
p: The prophets promised Jerusalem new names. Baruch's two names join peace with righteousness and glory with godliness.
b: Isaiah promised a new name from God's own mouth (Isaiah 62:2). Jeremiah gives one: "The LORD is our righteousness" (Jeremiah 33:16); Ezekiel another: "The LORD Is There" (Ezekiel 48:35). Baruch's names are a pair: peace that comes from righteousness, and glory that comes from fearing God. The Greek theosebeia, "godliness", means reverent worship of God; the KJV renders it "The glory of God's worship". A city named so would show the nations what the law (4:1) can make of a people.
orig: εἰρήνη δικαιοσύνης καὶ δόξα θεοσεβείας (eirēnē dikaiosynēs kai doxa theosebeias)

a: Get up, Jerusalem! Stand on the heights.
t: The Psalms of Solomon say it too
p: 5:5-8 runs very close to Psalms of Solomon 11. Scholars do not agree which borrowed from the other.
b: The Greek of Psalms of Solomon 11, a Jewish psalm collection of the first century BC, says "Stand, Jerusalem, on a height, and see your children from east and west gathered" (Psalms of Solomon 11:2–3), then that God lowered the high mountains "to level ground", that "the woods gave them shade", and that God made "every fragrant tree" spring up for them (Psalms of Solomon 11:4–7). Baruch 5:5–8 has the same pictures, many in the same Greek words. Toy dated the Psalms of Solomon to about 48 BC and left the direction open: "whichever may have been the borrower". Both are built from Isaiah 40 and 60.

a: lifted high in glory
p: They left on foot as prisoners; they come back carried, as Isaiah says the nations will carry Zion's children.
b: Isaiah: the nations "will bring your sons held close to their chests, and your daughters will ride on their shoulders" (Isaiah 49:22), and "your daughters are carried at the hip" (Isaiah 60:4). Baruch contrasts the march into exile, "on foot, with enemies driving them", with the return, "lifted high in glory". The picture of the returning children as a king's throne is the reading of Codex Vaticanus; other manuscripts have "like royal children" (see the variant).

a: every high mountain is to be brought low
p: Isaiah 40's road for God becomes the road for the returning exiles.
b: Isaiah: "Each valley will rise up, and each mountain and hill sink low. The steep ground will turn into flat land" (Isaiah 40:4), a highway for God in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3). Luke quotes the lines for John the Baptist: "Every ravine will be filled up, and every mountain and hill will be brought low" (Luke 3:5). In Baruch the road is for Israel, "so that Israel may walk safely in the glory of God". The Greek homalismos, "leveling", is also the word of Psalms of Solomon 11:5.
r: Isaiah 40:3–5; Luke 3:4–6; Isaiah 35:8; Isaiah 45:2; Psalms of Solomon 11:5

a: the age-old dunes
p: The Greek thines aenaoi are "ever-flowing" or "everlasting" heaps: sand dunes or banks.
b: Thīs is a heap or bank of sand, often a dune or a beach. Aenaos means "ever-flowing" or "everlasting". The KJV has "banks of long continuance", the Latin "everlasting rocks". The point is that even what seems most lasting in the landscape will give way to make a road.
orig: θῖνας ἀενάους (thinas aenaous)

a: every sweet-smelling tree
p: In Isaiah God plants trees in the desert. Here the woods shade Israel on the road home.
b: "In the wilderness I will put the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle and the olive" (Isaiah 41:19), and "every tree in the countryside will clap its hands" (Isaiah 55:12). Psalms of Solomon 11:6–7 has the woods giving shade and every fragrant tree. In 1:12 the exiles hoped to live "in the shade" of Babylon's kings; at the end it is God's trees that give shade.

a: God will lead Israel in gladness
t: Led by the light of glory
p: God leads the return as he led the Exodus, going ahead with his glory.
b: At the Exodus God went ahead of Israel in a pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21). Isaiah promises the returning exiles that "the LORD will go ahead of you, and the God of Israel will guard your rear" (Isaiah 52:12). The book ends on gladness, mercy and righteousness, the words that answer its beginning: "Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God" (1:15), and now he gives it to his people.
